title: SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO and RELEASE
learningObjectives: Create a named savepoint inside a transaction.
Use ROLLBACK TO to undo only work after a savepoint.
Use RELEASE to remove a savepoint marker.
Explain why releasing a savepoint does not commit the outer transaction.
Design a partial-recovery workflow for optional database work.

understand.concept: A savepoint marks a named position inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO returns the transaction to that position without ending the outer transaction. RELEASE removes the savepoint marker; the outer transaction still needs COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
understand.whyItMatters: Savepoints support partial recovery inside a larger operation, allowing an application to undo one optional step while keeping earlier valid work.
understand.analogy: A transaction is like a sealed work packet: its related steps are accepted together or returned for correction.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL locking, isolation levels, storage durability or engine-specific transaction implementation.

explain.narrative:
## Savepoints
SAVEPOINT name creates a named marker within the current transaction. ROLLBACK TO name undoes work performed after that marker while leaving the outer transaction active. RELEASE name removes the marker.

## Nested work is not an independent commit
SQLite savepoints can be nested. Releasing an inner savepoint does not commit the outer transaction. The outermost transaction is completed by COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

## Practical workflow
Use a savepoint around an optional sub-operation. If it fails, roll back to the savepoint and continue with the valid outer work. If it succeeds, release the savepoint and commit the transaction when all required work is complete.

### Savepoint scope
SAVEPOINT creates a named rollback marker within the current transaction. ROLLBACK TO rewinds changes made after the marker but keeps the transaction open. RELEASE removes the marker; releasing the outermost savepoint can complete the transaction, but releasing an inner savepoint does not commit the outer transaction.

### Practical use
Use savepoints for optional sub-operations that can fail independently while the main business operation remains valid. Give savepoints clear names, release them deliberately, and ensure the outer transaction still ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

examples.title: Create a table for staged work
examples.code: CREATE TABLE tx12_save_items (item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item_name TEXT NOT NULL, quantity INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO tx12_save_items VALUES (1, 'Base item', 10);
examples.explanation: Creates the table and inserts a baseline row. The baseline is outside the later transaction, so it should remain even when optional work is rolled back.

examples.title: Begin a transaction and add a required row
examples.code: BEGIN; INSERT INTO tx12_save_items VALUES (2, 'Required item', 5);
examples.explanation: Begins an outer transaction and inserts a required row. This row is before the savepoint and therefore remains after a rollback to that later marker.

examples.title: Create a savepoint before optional work
examples.code: SAVEPOINT optional_step; INSERT INTO tx12_save_items VALUES (3, 'Optional item', 2);
examples.explanation: Creates a named savepoint, then inserts optional work. The savepoint marks the point to which the current transaction can partially rewind; it is not an independent nested commit.

examples.title: Roll back only the optional work and release the marker
examples.code: ROLLBACK TO optional_step; RELEASE optional_step; SELECT item_id, item_name FROM tx12_save_items ORDER BY item_id;
examples.explanation: ROLLBACK TO removes the optional row but leaves the outer transaction active. RELEASE removes the savepoint marker, and the SELECT shows the baseline and required rows still present.

examples.title: Commit the outer transaction
examples.code: COMMIT; SELECT COUNT(*) AS saved_rows FROM tx12_save_items;
examples.explanation: Commits the outer transaction and counts the saved rows. The count of two confirms that the baseline and required row were committed while the optional row was discarded.

practise.guidedTask: Insert a required row, create a savepoint, insert an optional row, roll back to the savepoint, release it, and commit the required work.
practise.independentTask: Build a transaction that records an order and then attempts an optional discount allocation. Use a savepoint so the order can still be committed if the discount step is abandoned.
hints: A savepoint exists inside an outer transaction.
ROLLBACK TO keeps the outer transaction active.
RELEASE removes a savepoint marker but does not commit the outer transaction.
After rollback to a savepoint, release it when no longer needed.
Finish the outer transaction with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.prompt: Which statement creates a named savepoint?
questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT creates a named marker within the active transaction.

options: Undo changes after a savepoint while keeping the outer transaction active
questions.answer: Undo changes after a savepoint while keeping the outer transaction active
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK TO returns to the savepoint and leaves the outer transaction active.

questions.prompt: Does RELEASE savepoint commit the outer transaction?
options: Only when the savepoint is named main
Only when no rows were inserted
questions.explanation: RELEASE removes the marker; the outer transaction still needs COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.prompt: What is a useful savepoint use case?
options: Undo an optional sub-operation while preserving earlier required work
Back up the entire database file
questions.answer: Undo an optional sub-operation while preserving earlier required work
questions.explanation: Savepoints allow partial recovery inside a larger transaction.

questions.prompt: How is the outer transaction completed after savepoint work?
questions.explanation: The outer transaction still needs an explicit completion statement.
